frameworks.name: Give-to-Ask Ratio
frameworks.definition: A governance rule for content-based businesses specifying that public content (giving) must outweigh commercial asks (asking) by at least 3:1 to preserve audience goodwill; the optimal target for compounding growth is 30:1.

frameworks.name: Give Until They Ask Framework
frameworks.definition: A modified give-ask model where the creator withholds all asks until the audience proactively requests the offer, replacing scheduled asks with audience-initiated demand as the conversion trigger.

frameworks.name: Integrated vs Intermittent Ask Format
frameworks.definition: Two distinct commercial placement strategies: integrated asks are embedded naturally within long-form content (books, videos, podcasts); intermittent asks appear between discrete short-form posts (Instagram, TikTok) at a frequency of roughly 1-in-10 posts.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the primary reason audiences shrink after creators increase ask frequency is that each commercial ask is paid for in goodwill, not money. When a creator asks too often relative to how much they give, they overdraft the audience goodwill account and listenership drops.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator monetizing through public content (podcast, video, social media)
audience formed around informational or entertainment content
claims.mechanism: Each ask costs goodwill. When asks accumulate faster than value delivery replenishes goodwill, the audience perceives the channel as primarily commercial and reduces engagement.
bounded_by: Does not apply to paid subscription platforms where the audience has pre-consented to commercial content
Does not apply to direct-response ad placements purchased outside the organic content feed

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that major media platforms have empirically calibrated the give-to-ask ratio at approximately 3.6:1 (roughly 3-to-1). Television runs 47 minutes of content to 13 minutes of advertising per 60-minute slot. Facebook displays one ad per approximately four posts.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: commercial broadcast television (60-minute slot)
Facebook organic feed
bounded_by: These are platform-enforced maxima; Hormozi personally targets 98:2 (49:1) as his preferred ratio

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims his preferred personal give-to-ask ratio is approximately 98% give and 2% ask for video content, and no more than 3% ask frequency for short-form platforms (roughly one promotional post per 33 posts). For early-stage creators who want to prioritize growth, he recommends a 30:1 ratio.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator at growth stage who wants audience compounding
short-form platforms (Instagram, TikTok)
claims.mechanism: Holding asks below 3% preserves compounding: audience compounds when new members keep joining and existing members do not leave due to over-commercialization.

numbers.axis: creator give-to-ask ratio by platform type

bounded_by: For creators who need immediate income, the minimum viable ratio is 3:1 (television standard)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that integrated asks (embedded naturally within long-form content such as books, videos, and podcasts) perform better than intermittent asks for long-form platforms, while intermittent asks (one post per 10-33 posts appearing between content) are the correct format for short-form platforms such as Instagram and TikTok.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: long-form platforms: books, videos, podcasts, blog posts
short-form platforms: Instagram posts, TikTok reels
claims.mechanism: Long-form content consumption is a single extended session so inline integration adds a small percentage to total consume time; short-form posts are discrete units and an ask-post interrupts a streak of value posts, making intermittent placement the equivalent of an episode break rather than mid-episode commercial.

numbers.axis: recommended ask frequency by platform type

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the audience itself is the compounding asset, not individual pieces of content. Each piece of content functions as a one-time acquisition event that adds people permanently to the audience base, and those new audience members remain as long as the creator does not overdraft goodwill by asking too often.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator publishing consistent value-first content
give-to-ask ratio maintained above 10:1
claims.mechanism: Individual content pieces disappear from feeds in days but the people they attract remain permanently subscribed. The subscriber base compounds because each new piece adds subscribers without removing old ones, provided commercial pressure stays low.
bounded_by: Audience compounding stops if commercial frequency exceeds audience tolerance, causing unsubscribes that offset new additions

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that delaying commercial asks over time increases their eventual value nonlinearly, because audience size compounds. He estimates the value of a deferred ask could be 10 to 100 times larger 12 to 24 months later than if taken immediately.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator or business owner with a growing public audience
audience compounding trajectory in progress
claims.mechanism: Audience size compounds nonlinearly as each new member further accelerates content discovery. An endorsement or product launch made against a 10x larger audience produces proportionally larger revenue, so the opportunity cost of asking early is disproportionately large.

numbers.axis: multiplier on deferred ask value by wait period

bounded_by: Only applies when audience is still on a compounding growth curve
Does not apply to mature audiences with flat or declining growth rates

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that content creators who give consistently in public and sell in private build reputation in a self-reinforcing loop: public giving forces content quality because the brand is at stake, which attracts more audience, which compounds the value of the eventual ask.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: give in public, sell in private
conditions: creator with a public content channel and a separate private conversion mechanism (DMs, website, consultation)
claims.mechanism: Because selling happens privately, the public channel retains a pure-value reputation. This reputation signal attracts new audience members who have not been exposed to commercial asks, accelerating compounding. The separation also forces the creator to maintain content quality to preserve brand.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the business model requires public price display (e-commerce, SaaS with public pricing pages)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that demand-supply management via content is the strongest driver of pricing power: content artificially shifts the demand curve upward by increasing the number of people who want to buy, while the founder controls supply by limiting capacity. When demand exceeds supply, prices rise.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business with a capacity constraint the founder actively maintains
demand driven by public content audience
claims.mechanism: Content creation expands the pool of people aware of and wanting the offer (demand side). The founder controls intake (supply side). When demand persistently exceeds supply, buyers compete for access, which permits price increases without conversion loss.
bounded_by: Requires the founder to actually restrict supply; if supply expands to meet demand the pricing power effect disappears

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's goal for his content strategy is to attract businesses generating $1 million to $10 million in annual profit (not revenue) so that he can invest in them and help them grow. He reports that this outcome actually materialized from his content-first approach.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: content strategy: business/entrepreneurship education published on social media
target: owner-operated businesses at $1M-$10M annual profit

numbers.axis: annual profit of target business audience

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when an audience proactively asks a creator to offer something (inbound requests rather than outbound pitches), that is the signal that goodwill is sufficiently built and a commercial offer will convert without audience damage. He describes this as the give-until-they-ask trigger.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator has been publishing value-first content for an extended period
audience members proactively DM or comment asking for the creator's services or products
claims.mechanism: Inbound requests indicate that the audience has crossed the threshold where perceived value exceeds perceived price; the ask is likely to be received as a welcome answer rather than an interruption.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the first-post declaration of business (a public announcement that a creator is starting a business, paired with a free offer) is an effective first ask because the creator has accumulated goodwill with their existing social network over years, even without prior content creation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator has an existing social network (friends, family, colleagues, classmates) who have known them personally
creator has a demonstrated personal identity congruent with the business (e.g., always known as the fitness person)
claims.mechanism: Years of personal relationship serve as implicit value delivery. The social network has been receiving the creator's identity and knowledge informally; the declaration post formalizes what they already perceive as credible.
bounded_by: Effectiveness drops significantly if the business topic is incongruent with how the creator has been known to their network
Does not apply to creators with purely anonymous online-only audiences

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that he obtained his first 20 paying personal training clients from a single public declaration-of-business post in approximately April 2013, leveraging a decade of being known personally as someone obsessed with fitness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: existing personal social network with clear personal-brand congruence (fitness identity)
prior free value delivery: ~1 year of free training for clients who donated to charity

numbers.axis: clients acquired from first declaration post

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that having far more demand than supply is the single most important goal for a business owner, because persistent excess demand is what drives both pricing power and profit margins.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any business where price is not fixed by regulation or commodity market
claims.mechanism: When buyers compete for scarce capacity, the seller gains power to raise prices without losing demand. This shifts the business from price-taker to price-setter.
bounded_by: Does not apply to commodity or regulated markets where price is externally fixed

examples.text: A friend of Alex Hormozi who had a podcast that grew to millions of downloads saw rapid business growth, almost entirely from that audience. He noticed that making an ask on the podcast generated revenue, concluded that more asks would generate more revenue, and increased ask frequency. He initially made slightly more money, but then revenue declined and listenership dropped continuously as he overdrafted audience goodwill. Hormozi uses this story to illustrate the core danger of misreading ask frequency causality.

Alex Hormozi's April 2013 Facebook post (his first declaration of business) disclosed that he had spent nearly a year giving away free personal training to anyone willing to donate $500-$1,000 to a charity of their choice. The post announced he now had a website and a few roster slots open. This single post resulted in 20 paying clients messaging him. He attributes this to the long period of demonstrated results (before/after transformations visible online) and a lifetime of personal fitness identity that made the pivot credible to his network.

Alex Hormozi describes that when he began publishing business content on YouTube and Instagram, people quickly began DMing him asking for mentorship. He declined every request, reasoning that his audience was still growing and agreeing to mentor at that point would have capped his growth by locking him into a small-scale service model. By holding back, he preserved the compounding growth curve that eventually attracted $1M-$10M profit businesses to seek investment from Acquisition.com.

A friend of a friend had a tequila brand large enough that Dwayne Johnson (The Rock) approached him requesting two-thirds ownership. The owner declined. The Rock subsequently launched Teremana, which grew to a $6 billion brand. Hormozi uses this to illustrate that at the time of the offer, the owner's brand was still on a growth curve, and taking the deal might have been suboptimal relative to independent value creation. The story also illustrates the difficulty of timing commercial asks: what seems like leaving money on the table may be optimal given compounding.

practices.text: Give in public and sell in private. Keep your public content channel free of direct commercial asks and route all sales conversations to private channels (DMs, website, consultation calls).

For early-stage creators, make your first public post a declaration of business: announce what you are doing, offer something free, and invite interested people to reach out, without a hard commercial close.
Operationalize patience by figuring out what productive actions to take in the meantime rather than waiting passively. In business, patience means staying active in giving while deferring the ask.

When building a content audience, target maintaining far more demand than you have capacity to serve. Actively restrict supply (limit client intake, decline work) to sustain pricing power as demand grows.
For short-form platforms (Instagram, TikTok), limit promotional posts to no more than one in every ten posts (~10%), and aim for once or twice per month if posting multiple times daily.
